name: Garnet
workload: RESP-translated YCSB-A workload, 256M 8-byte keys, string values 8B-several KB, using memtier_benchmark and Garnet's own Resp.bench load generator against Garnet/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly on Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP networking
claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis): node throughput 108x, P99 latency at batch size 16 down to 0.25x; memtier GET throughput >=20x higher and P99 latency 3x lower than Valkey at high client load; up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly in some GET experiments; checkpoint speed 257x, scale-out (migration) speed 94x vs Redis
hardware: Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs, 72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 with accelerated TCP networking
stars_or_usage: 12k stars; described as widely deployed inside Microsoft
tradeoffs: Runs on the .NET runtime (GC, JIT) rather than being a native binary; kernel-bypass networking (eRPC/DPDK path) used for the best latency numbers is a prototype not shipped in the open-source build; complex RESP data types (SortedSet, HyperLogLog) add overhead
caveats: Evaluation performed and published by Garnet's own authors (Microsoft Research + Facebook/Meta-adjacent academics via VLDB peer review), not a fully independent third party, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) with full hardware/workload disclosure; memtier_benchmark itself became client-bottlenecked at high throughput so most headline figures use Garnet's own Resp.bench tool instead
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/FASTER README (deprecated, points to Garnet as successor) -> gh api repos/microsoft/garnet; VLDB paper fetched via WebFetch from https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf and read as PDF

name: Caffeine
workload: JMH microbenchmark (ComputeBenchmark/GetPutBenchmark) at 16 threads, varying read/write mixes (100% read, 75/25 read/write, 100% write) on a bounded in-process cache, vs ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache, Ehcache, Infinispan and plain ConcurrentHashMap
claimed_speedup: server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads): 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava, ~8.9x); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava, ~7.5x); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x)
hardware: Server-class: single-socket Xeon E5-2698B v3 @ 2.00GHz, 16 cores (hyperthreading disabled), 224GB RAM, Ubuntu 15.04, Azure G4 instance; desktop-class: MacBook Pro i7-4870HQ @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 17.9k stars; used as the cache implementation inside Spring, Cassandra, Solr and others
tradeoffs: In-process JVM cache, not a distributed/remote cache like Redis or Memcached, so it solves a different deployment problem (per-process hit ratio and speed rather than shared/networked state); W-TinyLFU admission policy adds bookkeeping vs a plain LRU
caveats: CPU model and OS are stated but the exact JVM version/flags used for the JMH run are not given in the wiki page as fetched; benchmark code and harness are public in the repo (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java) which is why this is scored B rather than C
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic cache --language c++ did not surface this; found via reasoning about 'LRU baselines the benchmark names' + gh api repos/ben-manes/caffeine, then WebFetch of the Benchmarks wiki page

name: Pelikan / Segcache
workload: NSDI'21 paper evaluation of Segcache (Pelikan's TTL-segmented storage engine) on production-derived cache workloads, scaling to 24 threads, comparing per-object metadata overhead and multi-core throughput scaling vs Memcached's slab allocator
claimed_speedup: ~8x higher throughput than Memcached at 24 threads; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes, cutting cache memory requirements 22-60% vs other state-of-the-art designs and 40-90% vs Pelikan's own prior slab storage
stars_or_usage: 295 stars (current Rust rewrite); legacy C implementation at github.com/twitter/pelikan has ~2k stars
tradeoffs: TTL-segmented design trades some flexibility (object grouping by expiry) for memory efficiency; original Segcache/legacy Pelikan was C, current pelikan-io/pelikan is a full Rust rewrite so the exact peer-reviewed binary is not what ships today
caveats: Numbers are quoted from the project's own blog restating its peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper; did not obtain the paper PDF directly in this session to confirm exact hardware/CPU model and compiler flags used in the formal evaluation, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/pelikan-io/pelikan; README opened directly, linking to Segcache blog and NSDI'21 paper page

name: Pogocache
workload: memtier_benchmark 100K SET + 100K GET ops per client, 256 clients over 16 I/O threads, pipelining 1/10/25/50, on AWS c8g.8xlarge (32-core ARM64), Unix socket, persistence off, 31 runs per point (median reported)
claimed_speedup: throughput ranking (pipeline 1, 8 threads): pogocache 3,145,960 ops/s vs memcache 2,601,306, garnet 1,548,050, dragonfly 1,407,584, valkey 1,331,683, redis 909,837 (~3.5x Redis, ~1.2x Memcached); lowest latency (111us) and fewest CPU cycles/op (6968) of the group
tradeoffs: Newer/less battle-tested than Redis/Memcached in production; supports Memcache, RESP and Postgres wire protocols but not full Redis command set (data structures, scripting, etc.)
caveats: The cache-benchmarks suite comparing pogocache to Redis/Valkey/Dragonfly/Garnet/Memcache is written and run by pogocache's own author (tidwall), so it is not a fully independent third party, even though the methodology (31 runs, median, stated hardware, stated versions) is unusually rigorous; exact compiler/build flags for each server are not listed, only released versions/commits
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/tidwall/pogocache; README table pointing to linked cache-benchmarks repo, opened directly

name: Dragonfly
workload: memtier_benchmark SET/GET ops (-d 256) against Redis on m5.large/m5.xlarge, and against Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge; also idle/peak memory usage during BGSAVE-equivalent snapshot
claimed_speedup: up to 25x throughput vs a single Redis process on c6gn.16xlarge (3.8M QPS); ~4.8x SET QPS vs Memcached (3844K vs 806K) on c6gn.16xlarge; ~30% more memory efficient than Redis at idle
hardware: AWS m5.large, m5.xlarge, c6gn.16xlarge, r6g/c7g (instance types stated; CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Business Source License restricts running it as a competing hosted service (converts to Apache-2.0 on 2030-11-01); single shared-nothing multi-threaded architecture differs operationally from Redis single-thread model
caveats: First-party README benchmark; AWS instance type given but exact CPU model, compiler, and build flags are not stated, so numbers cannot be independently reproduced from the README alone. A separate independent-ish suite (tidwall/cache-benchmarks) corroborates Dragonfly beating Redis/Memcached on AWS c8g.8xlarge with stated versions (see the Pogocache entry in this file).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/dragonflydb/dragonfly (seeded from prior knowledge of 'modern replacement for Redis and Memcached'); README benchmarks section opened directly

name: IKV (Inlined Key-Value Store)
workload: Multi-threaded client issuing blocking GET calls at fixed QPS levels (25K/50K/100K) against IKV (embedded, in-process) vs a 16-shard Redis Cluster on AWS ElastiCache; measuring avg/p50/p99 response time in microseconds
claimed_speedup: at 100K QPS: IKV avg 3.13us/p50 2.89us/p99 5.65us vs Redis Cluster avg 319us/p50 305us/p99 514us (roughly 100x lower average latency); README also claims embedded local Flash/SSD-backed IKV is still ~2x faster than an all-in-memory remote Redis cluster
tradeoffs: IKV is an embedded/in-process library colocated with the application (no network hop) rather than a shared remote cache, so much of the 100x gap is network round-trip elimination rather than a faster core engine; eventual consistency instead of Redis's stronger read-after-write guarantees; requires a separate data-plane (streams/object storage) to keep embedded replicas in sync
caveats: First-party README claim; linked full report is a Google Doc that could not be fully read in this session (only its title, 'IKV Perf Benchmarks | A comparison with Redis', was visible), so hardware/CPU model and compiler flags are unconfirmed; comparing an embedded cache against a networked cache is not entirely apples-to-apples for a 'faster engine' claim, though it is a legitimate real-workload latency win for the intended use case (ML feature serving)
found_via: HN Algolia: query 'faster than redis' -> 'IKV: embedded key-value store, 100x faster than Redis' (github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store); repo README opened directly

name: KeyDB
workload: memtier_benchmark, 32 threads over TLS, standard Redis GET/SET ops; benchmark client on AWS m5.8xlarge (32 cores), database instances on m5.4xlarge
claimed_speedup: over 7x faster than Redis with TLS enabled (~1M ops/s at 16 KeyDB threads vs ~130k ops/s for Redis 6 with TLS); Redis loses 36% throughput enabling TLS (61% with io-threads+TLS) while KeyDB shows almost no decline
hardware: AWS m5.8xlarge (client, 32 cores), m5.4xlarge (server instances) — CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Multithreading changes the concurrency/atomicity model vs Redis (MVCC-style access under a global lock for KEYS/SCAN); staying in sync with upstream Redis features is ongoing maintenance burden for a fork
caveats: First-party blog benchmark (KeyDB's own team); AWS instance type stated but not exact CPU model, compiler, or build flags; repository has had no commits in ~2.5 years even though the fork's changes are still substantive vs upstream Redis
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/Snapchat/KeyDB (seeded from prior knowledge of 'multithreaded fork of Redis'); README benchmark link opened directly

name: KVell
workload: YCSB core workloads (uniform and Zipfian key distributions), 1024B items, 100GB(100M keys)/5TB(5B keys) synthetic datasets, plus two Nutanix write-heavy (57:41:2 write:read:scan) production workloads, 250B-1KB items.
claimed_speedup: KVell achieves throughput at least 2x that of its closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, or WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads, and 5x on write-dominated workloads; tail latency an order of magnitude lower on scan-heavy workloads
hardware: Config-SSD: 32-core 2.4GHz Intel Xeon, 128GB RAM, 480GB Intel DC S3500 SSD; Config-Amazon-8NVMe: AWS i3.metal, 36x2 (72) cores at 2.3GHz, 488GB RAM, 8x1.9TB NVMe SSDs; Config-Optane: 4-core 4.2GHz Intel i7, 60GB RAM, 480GB Intel Optane 905P
tradeoffs: Shared-nothing architecture can suffer load imbalance; no in-memory sorted global index so scans are relatively weaker; designed around 4KB-atomic-write SSDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper states hardware in detail but compiler/flags were not found in the sections reviewed (intro, evaluation setup, IO design); repo's most recent commits look like housekeeping, core code dates to the 2019 paper.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "KVell" -> BLepers/KVell; paper PDF downloaded from repo and read directly

name: MatrixKV
workload: Random-write workload on a hybrid DRAM/NVM/SSD system using Intel Optane DC PMM, per the USENIX ATC'20 paper.
claimed_speedup: 3.6x higher random-write throughput and 5x lower 99th-percentile latency than RocksDB (also 2.6x/1.9x vs NoveLSM)
hardware: Intel Optane DC PMM (3D XPoint NVM) in a hybrid DRAM/NVM/SSD system
tradeoffs: Requires Intel Optane/PMDK-class NVM hardware to realize the reported gains; not a plain-SSD design.
caveats: Code is implemented as a diff against RocksDB v5.18.3 (not a GitHub fork, but explicitly derived, per repo instructions to `git reset --mixed` against that RocksDB commit); compiler/flags not stated on the paper abstract page viewed; repo unmaintained since 2020.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "MatrixKV" -> PDS-Lab/MatrixKV; paper page at usenix.org

name: PebblesDB
workload: db_bench-style single- and multi-threaded micro-benchmarks (50M KV pairs, 1KB values) plus a YCSB run (50M KV pairs, 1KB values, ~52GB user data) comparing PebblesDB, LevelDB, HyperLevelDB and RocksDB.
claimed_speedup: PebblesDB achieves 6x the write throughput of RocksDB, with similar read throughput and about 50% less IO (SOSP'17 peer-reviewed paper)
compiler_and_flags: Project states it 'was built, compiled, and tested with g++-4.7, g++-4.9, and g++-5' as a general build requirement; not confirmed as the exact compiler used for the cited benchmark run
tradeoffs: Write-optimized FLSM design trades away small-range-query performance on fully compacted stores; sequential-write throughput is lower than competitors.
caveats: benchmark.md does not itself state exact CPU model; the full SOSP'17 paper likely has it but was not opened in this session.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "LSM" "benchmark" language:C++ --sort stars

name: SplinterDB
workload: Insertion and point-query micro/macro-benchmarks on NVMe SSDs, per the USENIX ATC'20 paper 'SplinterDB: Closing the Bandwidth Gap for NVMe Key-Value Stores'.
claimed_speedup: 6-10x faster insertions and 2-2.6x faster point queries than RocksDB, with about 2x lower write amplification, while matching RocksDB on small range queries
tradeoffs: Project's own docs say it is not recommended for production before v1.0; gains are specifically tuned for NVMe device bandwidth characteristics.
caveats: Numbers taken from the USENIX ATC'20 paper's abstract/summary page; exact CPU model and compiler/flags used in the paper's full experiments were not verified in this session.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos + gh api repos/vmware/splinterdb, paper link cited in README

name: libmdbx
workload: General embedded read/write key-value operations; no specific benchmark harness, dataset size, or workload is described alongside the numbers.
claimed_speedup: README claims libmdbx is 'up to 10-100K times faster than both BoltDB and LMDB in particular extreme cases' and roughly 3x faster than BoltDB excluding disk I/O time
stars_or_usage: 1468 stars; README states it is 'used in hundreds of open source projects, including Ethereum'
tradeoffs: Uses shadow-paging/CoW instead of a WAL; no crash recovery step needed but long-lived read transactions can bloat the database.
caveats: No benchmark methodology, hardware, or compiler/flags stated; the '10-100K times faster' ratio is implausible on its face and self-reported, so tier is capped at C rather than higher.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/erthink/libmdbx (redirects to Mithril-mine/libmdbx), README section 'Comparison with other databases'

name: NuDB
workload: Insert N pseudo-random key/value pairs then fetch M random keys, at database sizes of 100,000 / 1,000,000 / 10,000,000 keys, per the project's own bench.cpp harness.
claimed_speedup: Sample table in repo: insert throughput 406598 vs 231937 ops/sec at 100K keys, 374330 vs 258519 at 1M keys (NuDB faster); fetch throughput 333443/337300 vs 34557/20835 ops/sec at 1M/10M keys (NuDB faster) but 325228 vs 697158 at 100K keys (NuDB slower) (numbers as printed on page)
tradeoffs: Append-only, insert-only design (no update/delete), all keys must be the same size; optimized specifically for random-read performance on SSDs, e.g. content-addressable storage.
caveats: The bench README explicitly labels the table 'a sample output', so it is unclear whether these are a captured real run or an illustrative example; no CPU model or compiler/flags are given.
found_via: GitHub: repo readme referencing RocksDB-based benchmarks -> bench/README.md

name: TerarkDB
workload: db_bench with 10 client threads, 20GB requests/thread, 24-byte keys and 2000-byte values; 'heavy_write' (90% write) and 'heavy_read' (90% read) mixes.
claimed_speedup: README shows a 'compare_rocksdb.png' graph of better throughput/tail-latency than RocksDB v6.12 across the heavy_write/heavy_read db_bench mixes; no single numeric ratio is given in the text
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 5218 CPU @ 2.30GHz (2 sockets, 32 cores / 64 threads), 376GB DRAM, NVMe TLC SSD (3.5TB)
tradeoffs: Fork of RocksDB v5.18.3 (data can migrate from RocksDB to TerarkDB but not back); only tested/production-ready on Linux.
caveats: TerarkDB is itself forked from RocksDB v5.18.3 but benchmarked against a newer RocksDB v6.12, so the two are different vintages; the result is presented only as a graph image, no extracted numeric ratio; compiler/flags unstated.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "LSM" "benchmark" language:C++ --sort stars

name: Titan (RocksDB plugin)
workload: 64GB dataset with 32GB memory limit, 1KB and 16KB value sizes, write- and update-heavy workloads (PingCap engineering blog benchmark).
claimed_speedup: About 70% higher write throughput and 180% higher update throughput than RocksDB, with gains increasing for larger values; underperforms RocksDB on range queries and has slightly higher space amplification
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 (40 cores), 128GB RAM, 1.5TB SATA SSD
stars_or_usage: 514 stars; used as a key-value-separation plugin inside TiKV
tradeoffs: Key-value separation (WiscKey-style) trades range-query performance and space amplification for write/update throughput, especially with large values.
caveats: First-party vendor (PingCap) blog post rather than an independent or peer-reviewed source; compiler/flags not stated.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "WiscKey" -> tikv/titan; blog post linked from README
